title: The Inflation Outlook and the Bond Market Sell-Off
gist: Capital Economics argues the October bond sell-off to mid-2000s highs in 10y UST yields is hard to justify on inflation alone: the rise is energy-driven, second-round effects are weak, and inflation should fall back in 2027, so central banks will tighten less than priced.

insights.claim: Global inflation rose from 2.6% y/y in January to 3.6% in August, driven almost entirely by energy; advanced-economy non-energy inflation was marginally lower in August than before the Iran war began.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: The inflation problem is a supply-shock story, not broad overheating.

insights.claim: Capital Economics forecasts Brent around $100 per barrel into early 2027 with elevated refining margins, pushing global inflation above 4% y/y in early 2027.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Expect headline inflation prints to worsen near term; energy and refiners remain supported.

insights.claim: The baseline assumes Middle East supply gradually improves in H1 2027, taking Brent to $70 by end-2027 and European gas to EUR40/MWh.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Gulf supply recovery is the key swing factor for the inflation and rates view.

insights.claim: Higher natural gas prices will lift household energy inflation across most advanced economies but not North America, where gas and power-generation costs have barely risen this year.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Energy inflation pain is regionally skewed toward Europe and Asia.

insights.claim: Energy costs will feed through to food and energy-intensive goods, pushing food inflation to multi-year highs in most developed economies, slowing rather than preventing disinflation.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Food-price pressure is a lagging effect to watch for consumer staples and politics.

insights.claim: Second-round effects are judged relatively low-risk because labour markets are less tight than in 2022 and firms report weaker demand, limiting wage catch-up and price pass-through despite higher household inflation expectations.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Supports the case that core inflation will not de-anchor.

insights.claim: Core inflation is expected to stay below 3% in major developed economies and fall toward 2% by end-2027, with US underlying pressure stronger partly because of the AI boom's effect on consumer technology prices.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: The US is the most likely place for sticky core inflation.

insights.claim: Capital Economics' headline inflation forecasts sit below two-year inflation swap rates and in most cases below consensus for 2028; the gap is largest in China, where excess-capacity deflation should reassert itself.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: A view that inflation breakevens are overpriced, especially the China deflation gap.

insights.claim: The Fed, ECB and Bank of England are expected to tighten over coming months but by less than markets price, so the recent rise in bond yields looks difficult to justify on the inflation outlook alone.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Argues for fading the sell-off in duration if energy supply does not deteriorate.

insights.claim: Risks are skewed one way: a deeper or more prolonged Gulf energy disruption would push inflation higher and force more aggressive central bank tightening.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: The bond call is effectively a bet on Gulf supply normalization.

insights.claim: 10-year US Treasury yields hit their highest level since the mid-2000s earlier this month, alongside hotter-than-expected September US inflation.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Sets the level and backdrop for the rates debate.

insights.claim: The firm remains optimistic on AI productivity but finds it increasingly hard to see returns justifying the scale of the past year's investment surge, particularly the debt financing behind it.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: AI-capex debt financing is a market-wide worry alongside bonds.

insights.claim: Stephen Brown argues AI-related activity has accounted for just over a quarter of US GDP growth over the past year.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: US growth is highly exposed to AI capex continuing.
